claim: The rare mitofusin (MFN) 2 R400Q mutation is 15–20× over-represented in clinical cardiomyopathy.
source: Here, we determined that the rare mitofusin (MFN) 2 R400Q mutation is 15–20× over-represented in clinical cardiomyopathy, whereas this specific mutation is not reported as a cause of MFN2 mutant-induced peripheral neuropathy, Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis comparing the frequency of the R400Q mutation in cardiomyopathy populations versus control databases (gnomAD), showing 15-20 fold over-representation with p<0.00001.

claim: The MFN2 R400Q mutation is not reported as a cause of MFN2 mutant-induced peripheral neuropathy, Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A).
source: Here, we determined that the rare mitofusin (MFN) 2 R400Q mutation is 15–20× over-represented in clinical cardiomyopathy, whereas this specific mutation is not reported as a cause of MFN2 mutant-induced peripheral neuropathy, Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A).
evidence: The manuscript states this as an observation from the literature review and clinical databases.

claim: All MFN2 mutants (T105M, M376A, R400Q) had impaired mitochondrial fusion.
source: All MFN2 mutants had impaired mitochondrial fusion, the canonical MFN2 function.
evidence: Figure 1D and 1E show experimental data measuring mitochondrial aspect ratio in cells expressing different MFN2 mutants, demonstrating reduced fusion activity compared to wild-type.

claim: MFN2 T105M lacks catalytic GTPase activity.
source: Compared to MFN2 T105M that lacked catalytic GTPase activity and exhibited normal activation-induced changes in conformation, MFN2 R400Q and M376A had normal GTPase activity with impaired conformational shifting.
evidence: Figure 2A shows GTPase activity measurements where T105M exhibits significantly reduced activity compared to wild-type MFN2.

claim: MFN2 T105M exhibited normal activation-induced changes in conformation.
source: Compared to MFN2 T105M that lacked catalytic GTPase activity and exhibited normal activation-induced changes in conformation, MFN2 R400Q and M376A had normal GTPase activity with impaired conformational shifting.
evidence: Figure 3A shows FRET studies demonstrating that T105M responds normally to antagonist and agonist peptides that induce conformational changes.

claim: MFN2 R400Q and M376A had normal GTPase activity.
source: Compared to MFN2 T105M that lacked catalytic GTPase activity and exhibited normal activation-induced changes in conformation, MFN2 R400Q and M376A had normal GTPase activity with impaired conformational shifting.
evidence: Figure 2A shows GTPase activity measurements where R400Q and M376A exhibit activity levels comparable to wild-type MFN2.

claim: MFN2 R400Q and M376A had impaired conformational shifting.
source: Compared to MFN2 T105M that lacked catalytic GTPase activity and exhibited normal activation-induced changes in conformation, MFN2 R400Q and M376A had normal GTPase activity with impaired conformational shifting.
evidence: Figure 3A shows FRET studies demonstrating that R400Q and M376A do not respond to antagonist and agonist peptides that normally induce conformational changes.

claim: MFN2 R400Q did not suppress mitochondrial motility.
source: MFN2 R400Q did not suppress mitochondrial motility, provoke mitochondrial depolarization, or dominantly suppress mitochondrial respiration like MFN2 T105M.
evidence: Figure 3B shows mitochondrial motility measurements in dorsal root ganglion neurons where R400Q does not reduce motility compared to wild-type.

claim: MFN2 R400Q did not provoke mitochondrial depolarization.
source: MFN2 R400Q did not suppress mitochondrial motility, provoke mitochondrial depolarization, or dominantly suppress mitochondrial respiration like MFN2 T105M.
evidence: Figure 2B shows TMRE staining demonstrating that R400Q does not cause loss of mitochondrial membrane potential unlike T105M.

claim: MFN2 R400Q did not dominantly suppress mitochondrial respiration like MFN2 T105M.
source: MFN2 R400Q did not suppress mitochondrial motility, provoke mitochondrial depolarization, or dominantly suppress mitochondrial respiration like MFN2 T105M.
evidence: Figure 2C shows Seahorse oxygen consumption measurements where R400Q maintains higher respiration levels than T105M, though lower than wild-type.

claim: MFN2 R400Q was uniquely defective in recruiting Parkin to mitochondria compared to MFN2 T105M and M376A.
source: By contrast to MFN2 T105M and M376A, MFN2 R400Q was uniquely defective in recruiting Parkin to mitochondria.
evidence: Figure 3C shows mcParkin recruitment assays where R400Q significantly reduces Parkin translocation to mitochondria after FCCP treatment, while T105M and M376A do not.

claim: CRISPR editing of the R400Q mutation into the mouse Mfn2 gene induced perinatal cardiomyopathy with no other organ involvement.
source: CRISPR editing of the R400Q mutation into the mouse Mfn2 gene induced perinatal cardiomyopathy with no other organ involvement; knock-in of Mfn2 T105M or M376V did not affect the heart.
evidence: Figure 4C-E shows survival data, histology, and electron microscopy demonstrating cardiac-specific pathology in Q/Q400 mice during the perinatal period.

claim: Knock-in of Mfn2 T105M or M376V did not affect the heart.
source: CRISPR editing of the R400Q mutation into the mouse Mfn2 gene induced perinatal cardiomyopathy with no other organ involvement; knock-in of Mfn2 T105M or M376V did not affect the heart.
evidence: Figure 4A-B shows genotyping data and the text describes that M376V mice had normal hearts and T105M heterozygotes had normal hearts (homozygotes were embryonic lethal).

claim: RNA sequencing and metabolomics of cardiomyopathic Mfn2 Q/Q400 hearts revealed signature abnormalities recapitulating experimental mitophagic cardiomyopathy.
source: RNA sequencing and metabolomics of cardiomyopathic Mfn2 Q/Q400 hearts revealed signature abnormalities recapitulating experimental mitophagic cardiomyopathy.
evidence: Figure 5 shows RNA-seq and metabolomics data from Q/Q400 hearts with downregulation of metabolic pathways similar to those observed in experimental mitophagy-deficient models cited in the text (Gong et al., 2015).

claim: Cultured cardiomyoblasts expressing MFN2 Q400 had mitophagy defects.
source: Indeed, cultured cardiomyoblasts and in vivo cardiomyocytes expressing MFN2 Q400 had mitophagy defects with increased sensitivity to doxorubicin.
evidence: Figure 6 shows time-course experiments in H9c2 cardiomyoblasts demonstrating delayed Parkin recruitment, autophagosome engulfment, and mitolysosome formation in cells expressing Q400.

claim: In vivo cardiomyocytes expressing MFN2 Q400 had mitophagy defects with increased sensitivity to doxorubicin.
source: Indeed, cultured cardiomyoblasts and in vivo cardiomyocytes expressing MFN2 Q400 had mitophagy defects with increased sensitivity to doxorubicin.
evidence: Figure 7E-G shows echocardiography, heart weights, and mitolysosome formation data demonstrating that Q/Q400 mice have worse cardiac outcomes and reduced mitophagy after doxorubicin treatment.

claim: MFN2 R400Q is the first known natural mitophagy-defective MFN2 mutant.
source: MFN2 R400Q is the first known natural mitophagy-defective MFN2 mutant.
evidence: The manuscript presents comprehensive data showing R400Q specifically impairs Parkin recruitment and mitophagy while other natural CMT2A mutants do not, and states this is the first such natural mutation identified.

claim: The unique profile of dysfunction of MFN2 R400Q evokes mitophagic cardiomyopathy.
source: Its unique profile of dysfunction evokes mitophagic cardiomyopathy, suggesting a mechanism for enrichment in clinical cardiomyopathy.
evidence: The manuscript presents multiple lines of evidence including in vitro mitophagy assays, knock-in mouse phenotypes, and transcriptional/metabolic signatures that collectively support this conclusion.

claim: Hearts rely upon mitochondria-derived ATP to fuel cardiac development, excitation–contraction–coupling, and myocardial repair after damage or senescence.
source: Hearts rely upon mitochondria-derived ATP to fuel cardiac development, excitation–contraction–coupling, and myocardial repair after damage or senescence.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction without specific citation, representing general scientific consensus.

claim: Cardiac involvement is common in diseases like MELAS and MERRF caused by genetic defects of the mitochondrial genome (mtDNA).
source: For this reason, cardiac involvement is common in diseases like MELAS and MERRF caused by genetic defects of the mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) (Hsu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hsu et al., 2016.

claim: The vast majority of the ~1000 constituent mitochondrial proteins are not encoded by mtDNA, but instead by nuclear genes.
source: However, the vast majority of the ~1000 constituent mitochondrial proteins are not encoded by mtDNA, but instead by nuclear genes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mitofusins (MFN) 1 and 2 are nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins having central roles in mitochondrial health and homeostasis.
source: Among nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins having central roles in mitochondrial health and homeostasis are mitofusins (MFN) 1 and 2 (Santel and Fuller, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Santel and Fuller, 2001.

claim: Cardiac MFNs are critical mediators of reparative mitochondrial fusion.
source: Gene ablation and mutant transgene expression studies targeting cardiac myocytes indicate that cardiac MFNs are critical mediators of reparative mitochondrial fusion (Chen et al., 2011; Kasahara et al., 2013), mitochondrial culling for quality control (Song et al., 2015; Song et al., 2017), and mitochondrial replacement for metabolic plasticity (Gong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2011 and Kasahara et al., 2013.

claim: Cardiac MFNs are critical mediators of mitochondrial culling for quality control.
source: Gene ablation and mutant transgene expression studies targeting cardiac myocytes indicate that cardiac MFNs are critical mediators of reparative mitochondrial fusion (Chen et al., 2011; Kasahara et al., 2013), mitochondrial culling for quality control (Song et al., 2015; Song et al., 2017), and mitochondrial replacement for metabolic plasticity (Gong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Song et al., 2015 and Song et al., 2017.

claim: Cardiac MFNs are critical mediators of mitochondrial replacement for metabolic plasticity.
source: Gene ablation and mutant transgene expression studies targeting cardiac myocytes indicate that cardiac MFNs are critical mediators of reparative mitochondrial fusion (Chen et al., 2011; Kasahara et al., 2013), mitochondrial culling for quality control (Song et al., 2015; Song et al., 2017), and mitochondrial replacement for metabolic plasticity (Gong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gong et al., 2015.

claim: Cardiac involvement has not been reported in human conditions caused by natural loss-of-function MFN gene mutations.
source: On the other hand, cardiac involvement has not been reported in human conditions caused by natural loss-of-function MFN gene mutations.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the literature, representing a gap in reported clinical phenotypes.

claim: Dozens of different pathological MFN2 mutations cause neuronal rather than cardiac pathology, manifested as Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A).
source: Indeed, dozens of different pathological MFN2 mutations cause neuronal rather than cardiac pathology, manifested as Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A) (Züchner et al., 2004) or optic degeneration (Züchner et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Züchner et al., 2004 and Züchner et al., 2006.

claim: Mitochondrial motility defects induced by mutant MFN2 are responsible for clinical neuropathies because neurons have long axonal and dendritic processes that make them critically dependent upon mitochondrial transport.
source: We have proposed that mitochondrial motility defects induced by mutant MFN2 are responsible for clinical neuropathies because neurons have long axonal and dendritic processes that make them critically dependent upon mitochondrial transport (Dorn, 2019; Dorn, 2021).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis proposed by the authors in previous work, supported by citations to Dorn, 2019 and Dorn, 2021.

claim: Impaired mitophagy seems to underlie developmental and senescent cardiomyopathies provoked by Mfn gene ablation or engineered MFN2 mutant expression.
source: By contrast, impaired mitophagy seems to underlie developmental and senescent cardiomyopathies provoked by Mfn gene ablation or engineered MFN2 mutant expression (Bhandari et al., 2014; Gong et al., 2015; Dorn, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bhandari et al., 2014; Gong et al., 2015; and Dorn, 2016.

claim: MFN2 multifunctionality reflects its ability to bind different protein partners as determined by specific phosphorylation events.
source: MFN2 multifunctionality reflects its ability to bind different protein partners as determined by specific phosphorylation events (Dorn, 2020; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dorn, 2020 and Li et al., 2022.

claim: MFN2 oligomerization with MFN1 or MFN2 mediates mitochondrial fusion.
source: Thus, MFN2 oligomerization with MFN1 or MFN2 mediates mitochondrial fusion (Chen et al., 2010; Dorn and Dang, 2022), MFN2 binding of Parkin mediates mitophagy (Chen and Dorn, 2013; Li et al., 2022), and MFN2 binding to Miro regulates mitochondrial transport (Misko et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2010 and Dorn and Dang, 2022.

claim: MFN2 binding of Parkin mediates mitophagy.
source: Thus, MFN2 oligomerization with MFN1 or MFN2 mediates mitochondrial fusion (Chen et al., 2010; Dorn and Dang, 2022), MFN2 binding of Parkin mediates mitophagy (Chen and Dorn, 2013; Li et al., 2022), and MFN2 binding to Miro regulates mitochondrial transport (Misko et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen and Dorn, 2013 and Li et al., 2022.

claim: MFN2 binding to Miro regulates mitochondrial transport.
source: Thus, MFN2 oligomerization with MFN1 or MFN2 mediates mitochondrial fusion (Chen et al., 2010; Dorn and Dang, 2022), MFN2 binding of Parkin mediates mitophagy (Chen and Dorn, 2013; Li et al., 2022), and MFN2 binding to Miro regulates mitochondrial transport (Misko et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Misko et al., 2010.

claim: A total of 352 rare nonsynonymous MFN2 variants are reported in the gnomAD database (MAF 3.98E-06–6.87 E-03).
source: A total of 352 rare nonsynonymous MFN2 variants are reported (MAF 3.98E-06–6.87 E-03) of which 171 are singletons.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the gnomAD database analysis.

claim: 76 of the rare MFN2 variants are implicated in CMT2A.
source: Notably, 76 of the rare MFN2 variants are implicated in CMT2A (Stuppia et al., 2015; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stuppia et al., 2015 and reference to supplementary data.

claim: 11 non-synonymous MFN2 variants were detected in the cardiomyopathy screening cohorts.
source: As summarized in Table 1, 11 non-synonymous MFN2 variants were detected, 6 of which encode putative CMT2A mutations.
evidence: Table 1 presents the screening results showing 11 variants identified.

claim: 6 of the 11 detected MFN2 variants encode putative CMT2A mutations.
source: As summarized in Table 1, 11 non-synonymous MFN2 variants were detected, 6 of which encode putative CMT2A mutations.
evidence: Table 1 shows which variants are annotated as CMT2A mutations in ClinVar.

claim: 8 of the 11 MFN2 variants were singletons.
source: Also, 8 of the 11 MFN2 variants were singletons and therefore of minimal interest.
evidence: Table 1 shows singleton status for the variants.

claim: MFN2 R400Q was detected in three unrelated individuals: two with HCM and one with DCM.
source: MFN2 R400Q, which is not a known CMT2A mutation and is bioinformatically predicted to be damaging, was detected in three unrelated individuals: two with HCM and one with DCM (Table 1).
evidence: Table 1 shows the distribution of R400Q across the study cohorts.

claim: MFN2 R400Q is bioinformatically predicted to be damaging.
source: MFN2 R400Q, which is not a known CMT2A mutation and is bioinformatically predicted to be damaging, was detected in three unrelated individuals: two with HCM and one with DCM (Table 1).
evidence: Table 1 shows Polyphen 2 prediction as 'Prob dam' (probably damaging).

claim: The MFN2 R400Q mutation is reported almost exclusively in African populations in the gnomAD database.
source: The MFN2 R400Q mutation (Figure 1A and B) is reported almost exclusively in African populations in the gnomAD database (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of gnomAD database population data.

claim: All three subjects with the R400Q variant in the cardiomyopathy study populations identified as African American.
source: Indeed, all three subjects with the R400Q variant in our cardiomyopathy study populations identified as African American.
evidence: This is reported from the study cohort demographic data.

claim: The overall MFN2 R400Q MAF of 0.0015 in cardiomyopathy represents ~20-fold over-representation compared to MAF of 0.000074 from the gnomAD database (p<0.00001).
source: The overall MFN2 R400Q MAF of 0.0015 in cardiomyopathy, when compared to MAF of 0.000074 from the gnomAD database, represents ~20-fold over-representation in the combined heart disease populations (p<0.00001).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of allele frequencies between the study cohort and gnomAD database.

claim: When comparing only to the gnomAD African-derived population, MFN2 R400Q over-representation was ~15-fold (p-value = 0.0033).
source: If only the gnomAD African-derived population is used to account for racial differences in R400Q prevalence (10/24,962), over-representation was ~15-fold (p-value = 0.0033).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison accounting for population stratification.

claim: None of the non-affected controls (625 Caucasian and 236 African American subjects) had the MFN2 R400Q mutation.
source: None of the non-affected controls (625 Caucasian and 236 African American subjects) had the MFN2 R400Q mutation.
evidence: This is reported from the control cohort screening results.

claim: A previous description of MFN2 R400Q showed impaired fusogenicity conferring retinal and myocardial abnormalities in transgenic Drosophila.
source: Because a previous description of this MFN2 mutant described impaired fusogenicity conferring retinal and myocardial abnormalities in transgenic Drosophila (Eschenbacher et al., 2012), we surmised that, like other loss-of-function MFN2 mutants (Flannick et al., 2014; Steinberg et al., 2015), MFN2 Q400 could have pathophysiological relevance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eschenbacher et al., 2012.

claim: Many CMT2A MFN2 mutations, including prototypical MFN2 T105M, are located within the GTPase domain and lack catalytic GTPase activity.
source: Many CMT2A MFN2 mutations, including prototypical MFN2 T105M, are located within the GTPase domain (Figure 1A, green region) and lack catalytic GTPase activity (Franco et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Franco et al., 2022 and Figure 1A showing mutation locations.

claim: MFN2 R400Q is located in the hydrophobic core within the first heptad repeat domain (HR1).
source: By contrast, MFN2 R400Q (Figure 1B) is located in the hydrophobic core within the so-called first heptad repeat domain (HR1; Figure 1A, red region).
evidence: Figure 1A shows the structural location of R400Q in the HR1 domain.

claim: The normal mitochondrial aspect ratio in wild-type murine embryonic fibroblasts is ~5–6.
source: The normal mitochondrial aspect ratio of ~5–6 in WT murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) is reduced to ~2 in MEFs lacking both mitofusins (Mfn DKO) (compare white bars in Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Figure 1E shows the baseline aspect ratio measurement in WT MEFs.

claim: Mitochondrial aspect ratio is reduced to ~2 in MEFs lacking both mitofusins (Mfn DKO).
source: The normal mitochondrial aspect ratio of ~5–6 in WT murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) is reduced to ~2 in MEFs lacking both mitofusins (Mfn DKO) (compare white bars in Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Figure 1D shows the baseline aspect ratio measurement in Mfn DKO MEFs.

claim: GTP hydrolysis is absolutely required for mitochondrial fusion.
source: Consistent with an absolute requirement for GTP hydrolysis during mitochondrial fusion, all three GTPase domain MFN2 mutants exhibited diminished fusogenicity compared to WT MFN2 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; left panel, green bars).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by the experimental data showing GTPase-defective mutants have impaired fusion.

claim: Intrinsic fusogenicity of MFN2 M376A and R400Q was similarly impaired.
source: Intrinsic fusogenicity of MFN2 M376A and R400Q was similarly impaired (Figure 1D, red bars).
evidence: Figure 1D shows comparable reductions in mitochondrial aspect ratio for both M376A and R400Q in DKO cells.

claim: Most CMT2A-associated MFN2 mutants dominantly suppress mitochondrial fusion mediated by normal mitofusins 1 and 2.
source: Most CMT2A-associated MFN2 mutants do not simply exhibit reduced intrinsic fusogenicity, but dominantly suppress mitochondrial fusion mediated by normal mitofusins 1 and 2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies and demonstrated by the experiments in Figure 1E.

claim: Expression of WT MFN2 in WT MEFs caused mitochondrial hyper-fusion, increasing mitochondrial aspect ratio to ~8.
source: As expected, expression of WT MFN2 caused mitochondrial hyper-fusion, increasing mitochondrial aspect ratio to ~8 (Figure 1E, black bar).
evidence: Figure 1E shows the aspect ratio measurement for WT MFN2 expressed in WT MEFs.

claim: All three GTPase domain MFN2 mutants and MFN2 R400Q suppressed normal mitochondrial fusion in WT cells.
source: By comparison, all three GTPase domain MFN2 mutants and MFN2 R400Q suppressed normal mitochondrial fusion (i.e. lowered mitochondrial aspect ratio vs. adeno-βgal transduced) in WT cells.
evidence: Figure 1E shows reduced aspect ratios for these mutants compared to the β-gal control in WT MEFs.

claim: MFN2 M376A did not alter baseline aspect ratio of WT MEF.
source: Uniquely among the expressed MFN2 mutants, MFN2 M376A did not alter baseline aspect ratio of WT MEF (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, right panel).
evidence: Figure 1E shows that M376A maintains an aspect ratio similar to the β-gal control in WT MEFs.

claim: MFN1 and MFN2 are dynamin family GTPases.
source: MFN1 and MFN2 are dynamin family GTPases; catalytic GTPase activity is required for mitochondrial fusion (Chan, 2006; Santel and Fuller, 2001; Franco et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chan, 2006; Santel and Fuller, 2001; and Franco et al., 2022.

claim: Catalytic GTPase activity is required for mitochondrial fusion.
source: MFN1 and MFN2 are dynamin family GTPases; catalytic GTPase activity is required for mitochondrial fusion (Chan, 2006; Santel and Fuller, 2001; Franco et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chan, 2006; Santel and Fuller, 2001; and Franco et al., 2022.

claim: Adenovirally expressed WT MFN2 accounted for approximately two-thirds of total mitochondrial GTPase activity in transduced mitofusin DKO cells.
source: Adenovirally expressed WT MFN2 accounted for approximately two-thirds of total mitochondrial GTPase activity in transduced mitofusin DKO cells (Figure 2A, black bar).
evidence: Figure 2A shows GTPase activity measurements comparing WT MFN2 to β-gal control.

claim: MFN2 T105M, R94Q, and K109A each lacked GTPase activity.
source: As expected, MFN2 T105M, R94Q, and K109A each lacked GTPase activity (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, left panel, green bars).
evidence: Figure 2A shows GTPase activity measurements for these mutants at levels comparable to β-gal control.

claim: GTPase activity of MFN2 R400Q and M376A was the same as WT MFN2.
source: Remarkably, GTPase activity of MFN2 R400Q and M376A was the same as WT MFN2, that is, normal (Figure 2A, red bars).
evidence: Figure 2A shows GTPase activity measurements for R400Q and M376A at levels comparable to WT MFN2.

claim: Diminished GTPase activity cannot be the mechanism for impaired fusogenicity of MFN2 HR1 domain mutants R400Q and M376A.
source: Thus, diminished GTPase activity cannot be the mechanism for impaired fusogenicity of these two MFN2 HR1 domain mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing these mutants have normal GTPase activity but impaired fusion.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration and oxidative phosphorylation of ADP to ATP are driven by an electrochemical gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: Mitochondrial respiration and oxidative phosphorylation of ADP to ATP are driven by an electrochemical gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane, the so-called 'proton pump' (Madeira, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Madeira, 2018.

claim: Dissipation of the inner membrane electrochemical gradient (mitochondrial depolarization) was provoked by MFN2 T105M, R94Q, and K109A.
source: Dissipation of the inner membrane electrochemical gradient (mitochondrial depolarization) was provoked by MFN2 T105M, R94Q, and K109A, but not by MFN2 M376A or R400Q (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, right panel).
evidence: Figure 2B shows TMRE staining results demonstrating loss of mitochondrial polarization for these GTPase-defective mutants.

claim: MFN2 M376A and R400Q did not provoke mitochondrial depolarization.
source: Dissipation of the inner membrane electrochemical gradient (mitochondrial depolarization) was provoked by MFN2 T105M, R94Q, and K109A, but not by MFN2 M376A or R400Q (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, right panel).
evidence: Figure 2B shows TMRE staining results demonstrating maintained mitochondrial polarization for these HR1 mutants.

claim: For MFN2 mutants, the ability to induce mitochondrial depolarization corresponds with impaired catalytic GTPase activity.
source: Thus, for these MFN2 mutants, the ability to induce mitochondrial depolarization corresponds with impaired catalytic GTPase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the GTPase activity data (Figure 2A) with the depolarization data (Figure 2B).

claim: Introducing WT MFN2 into cells lacking mitofusins enhanced all phases of mitochondrial respiration.
source: As expected, introducing WT MFN2 into cells lacking mitofusins enhanced all phases of mitochondrial respiration (Figure 2C, black).
evidence: Figure 2C shows Seahorse oxygen consumption measurements demonstrating increased basal, ATP-linked, and maximal respiration with WT MFN2.

claim: MFN2 T105M failed to enhance mitochondrial respiration.
source: By comparison, MFN2 T105M failed to enhance mitochondrial respiration (Figure 2C, green).
evidence: Figure 2C shows Seahorse oxygen consumption measurements for T105M at levels similar to β-gal control.

claim: MFN2 M376A and R400Q increased mitochondrial respiration vs. the complete absence of mitofusins, but not to the same extent as WT MFN2.
source: Strikingly, MFN2 M376A and R400Q were intermediate in their effects, increasing mitochondrial respiration vs. the complete absence of mitofusins (i.e. vs. β-gal), but seemingly not to the same extent as WT MFN2 (Figure 2C, red).
evidence: Figure 2C shows Seahorse oxygen consumption measurements for M376A and R400Q at intermediate levels between β-gal and WT MFN2.

claim: There is a central relationship between mitochondrial GTPase activity, polarization, and respiration.
source: These data provide further evidence supporting the central relationship between mitochondrial GTPase activity, polarization, and respiration.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective data in Figure 2 showing correlated patterns across these three measurements.

claim: Mitofusin protein conformation changes upon activation, transitioning from a closed basal state to an open state that favors mitochondrial fusion.
source: Mitofusin protein conformation changes upon activation, transitioning from a closed basal state to an open state that favors mitochondrial fusion (Franco et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Franco et al., 2016.

claim: The closed conformation of MFN2 is maintained by peptide–peptide interactions involving MFN2 amino acids 367–384 in the HR1 domain.
source: The closed conformation is maintained by peptide–peptide interactions involving MFN2 amino acids 367–384 in the HR1 domain (Rocha et al., 2018; Dorn, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rocha et al., 2018 and Dorn, 2019.

claim: GTPase-defective CMT2A mutant MFN2 T105M transitioned normally from open to closed state.
source: Consistent with this notion, GTPase-defective CMT2A mutant MFN2 T105M transitioned normally from open to closed state, as measured by antagonist and agonist peptide-induced changes in Forster resonance energy transfer (FRET; Dang et al., 2020; Figure 3A, green bars).
evidence: Figure 3A shows FRET measurements demonstrating normal conformational changes for T105M in response to peptides.

claim: The MFN2 M376A and R400Q FRET signals did not change in the presence of MFN antagonist and agonist peptides.
source: By contrast, the MFN2 M376A and R400Q FRET signals did not change in the presence of MFN antagonist and agonist peptides that normally provoke the closed or open conformation, respectively (Figure 3A, red bars; Franco et al., 2016).
evidence: Figure 3A shows FRET measurements demonstrating lack of conformational changes for M376A and R400Q in response to peptides.

claim: MFN2 HR1 domain mutants M376A and R400Q are defective in their ability to move between open fusion-permissive and closed fusion-limiting conformations.
source: Thus, these MFN2 HR1 domain mutants are defective in their ability to move between open fusion-permissive and closed fusion-limiting conformations, which can explain how mitochondrial fusion is impaired by these mutations despite normal catalytic GTPase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data showing lack of conformational switching in these mutants.

claim: Some CMT2A-linked MFN2 mutations dominantly suppress mitochondrial motility.
source: The appellative function of mitofusins is to mediate mitochondrial fusion, but MFN2 has additional non-canonical tasks including to promote mitochondrial transport (Misko et al., 2010; Rocha et al., 2018; Franco et al., 2020). Indeed, some CMT2A-linked MFN2 mutations dominantly suppress mitochondrial motility, thereby contributing to die-back of long peripheral nerves that require distal mitochondrial delivery for cell renewal and regeneration (Misko et al., 2010; Rocha et al., 2018; Franco et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Misko et al., 2010; Rocha et al., 2018; and Franco et al., 2020.

claim: Mitochondrial transport through neuronal processes was suppressed by GTPase-defective MFN2 mutants T105M and K109A.
source: Consistent with previous observations that mitochondrial fusion and motility can be co-regulated by MFN2 (Franco et al., 2022), mitochondrial transport through neuronal processes was suppressed by GTPase-defective MFN2 mutants T105M and K109A (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, green bar), and an MFN2 mutant engineered to mimic phosphorylation at sites that suppress mitochondrial fusion, MFN2 EE (Chen and Dorn, 2013; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, gray bar MFN2 E111, E442).
evidence: Figure 3B shows mitochondrial motility measurements in DRG neurons demonstrating reduced motility for these mutants.

claim: Mitochondrial motility in DRG neurons was unaffected by HR1 domain mutants M376A and R400Q.
source: Mitochondrial motility in DRG neurons was unaffected by HR1 domain mutants M376A and R400Q (Figure 3B, red bars) or by an MFN2 mutant engineered to prevent phosphorylation at the fusion-regulatory sites, MFN2 AA (Chen and Dorn, 2013; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, A111A442).
evidence: Figure 3B shows mitochondrial motility measurements in DRG neurons demonstrating normal motility for these mutants.

claim: Combined abnormalities of mitochondrial fusion and motility exhibited by GTPase-defective MFN2 mutants are dissociated in MFN2 HR1 domain mutants.
source: Thus, combined abnormalities of mitochondrial fusion and motility exhibited by GTPase-defective MFN2 mutants are dissociated in MFN2 HR1 domain mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the fusion data (Figure 1) with the motility data (Figure 3B) showing different patterns for GTPase vs. HR1 mutants.

claim: MFN2 can initiate mitophagy by switching from a fusion protein into a 'Parkin receptor' that recruits cytosolic Parkin to damaged mitochondria.
source: MFN2 can initiate mitophagy by switching from a fusion protein into a 'Parkin receptor' that recruits cytosolic Parkin to damaged mitochondria (Chen and Dorn, 2013; Xiong et al., 2019; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen and Dorn, 2013; Xiong et al., 2019; and Li et al., 2022.

claim: Mitophagic vs. fusogenic properties of MFN2 are determined by the phosphorylation status of MFN2 T111 and S442.
source: Mitophagic vs. fusogenic properties are determined by the phosphorylation status of MFN2 T111 and S442 (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2022.

claim: MFN2 functioning as a Parkin receptor and mitophagy effector is important to heart development and/or contractile function.
source: Prior studies have suggested that MFN2 functioning as a Parkin receptor and mitophagy effector is important to heart development and/or contractile function (Chen and Dorn, 2013; Gong et al., 2015; Song et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen and Dorn, 2013; Gong et al., 2015; and Song et al., 2015.

claim: Non-phosphorylated WT MFN2 promotes MFN-MFN-mediated fusion, but cannot bind Parkin.
source: Thus, non-phosphorylated WT MFN2 promotes MFN-MFN-mediated fusion, but cannot bind Parkin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior work on MFN2 phosphorylation-dependent function switching.

claim: MFN2 phosphorylation on S378 extinguishes fusion.
source: MFN2 phosphorylation on S378 extinguishes fusion (Rocha et al., 2018) and on T111 and S442 enables Parkin binding to initiate mitophagy (Chen and Dorn, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rocha et al., 2018.

claim: MFN2 phosphorylation on T111 and S442 enables Parkin binding to initiate mitophagy.
source: MFN2 phosphorylation on S378 extinguishes fusion (Rocha et al., 2018) and on T111 and S442 enables Parkin binding to initiate mitophagy (Chen and Dorn, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen and Dorn, 2013.

claim: MFN2 phosphorylation on T111 and S442 and its control of mitochondrial fate are mechanistically linked by altered MFN2 protein partnering as a consequence of phosphorylation-induced changes in MFN2 conformation.
source: MFN2 phosphorylation on these residues and its control of mitochondrial fate are mechanistically linked by altered MFN2 protein partnering as a consequence of phosphorylation-induced changes in MFN2 conformation (Dorn, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dorn, 2020.

claim: Parkin translocation in response to FCCP was unaffected by MFN2 WT, T105M, K109A, and M376A.
source: Parkin translocation in response to FCCP was unaffected by MFN2 WT, T105M, K109A, and M376A, but was markedly reduced in cells expressing MFN2 R400Q (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,+FCCP).
evidence: Figure 3C shows Parkin aggregation measurements after FCCP treatment demonstrating normal responses for these mutants.

claim: Parkin translocation in response to FCCP was markedly reduced in cells expressing MFN2 R400Q.
source: Parkin translocation in response to FCCP was unaffected by MFN2 WT, T105M, K109A, and M376A, but was markedly reduced in cells expressing MFN2 R400Q (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,+FCCP).
evidence: Figure 3C shows Parkin aggregation measurements after FCCP treatment demonstrating significantly reduced response for R400Q.

claim: Suppression of Parkin recruitment by MFN2 R400Q was similar in magnitude to that of MFN2AA.
source: Indeed, suppression of Parkin recruitment by MFN2 R400Q was similar in magnitude to that of MFN2AA (Chen and Dorn, 2013; Gong et al., 2015; Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, +FCCP).
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1C shows comparable levels of Parkin recruitment suppression for R400Q and AA mutants.

claim: MFN-mediated mitochondrial fusion is essential to early embryonic heart development.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that MFN-mediated mitochondrial fusion is essential to early embryonic heart development, and that MFN2-Parkin-mediated mitophagy is required for metabolic maturation of perinatal myocardium (Kasahara et al., 2013; Gong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kasahara et al., 2013.

claim: MFN2-Parkin-mediated mitophagy is required for metabolic maturation of perinatal myocardium.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that MFN-mediated mitochondrial fusion is essential to early embryonic heart development, and that MFN2-Parkin-mediated mitophagy is required for metabolic maturation of perinatal myocardium (Kasahara et al., 2013; Gong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gong et al., 2015.

claim: Heterozygous knock-in mice from each line (T105M, M376V, R400Q) were viable.
source: Heterozygous knock-in mice from each line were viable, and therefore interbred to expand colonies.
evidence: This is reported from the breeding experiments.

claim: Mutant allele frequency of offspring was significantly lower in Mfn2 T105M mice.
source: Mutant allele frequency of resulting offspring, expected to be ~50%, was significantly lower in Mfn2 T105M mice, and trended lower in Mfn2 R400Q mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: Figure 4A shows allele frequency data demonstrating significant deviation from expected Mendelian ratios for T105M.

claim: Mutant allele frequency of offspring trended lower in Mfn2 R400Q mice.
source: Mutant allele frequency of resulting offspring, expected to be ~50%, was significantly lower in Mfn2 T105M mice, and trended lower in Mfn2 R400Q mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: Figure 4A shows allele frequency data demonstrating a trend toward lower than expected frequency for R400Q.

claim: No homozygous mutant Mfn2 T105M mice were found at 7 days old.
source: Genotyping of 7-day-old pups revealed no homozygous mutant Mfn2 T105M mice and an abnormally low percentage of homozygous mutant Mfn2 R400Q mice, whereas mutant allele distribution of Mfn2 M376V mice followed Mendelian norms (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows genotype distribution data with zero homozygous T105M mice.

claim: An abnormally low percentage of homozygous mutant Mfn2 R400Q mice were found at 7 days old.
source: Genotyping of 7-day-old pups revealed no homozygous mutant Mfn2 T105M mice and an abnormally low percentage of homozygous mutant Mfn2 R400Q mice, whereas mutant allele distribution of Mfn2 M376V mice followed Mendelian norms (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows genotype distribution data with fewer than expected homozygous R400Q mice.

claim: Mutant allele distribution of Mfn2 M376V mice followed Mendelian norms.
source: Genotyping of 7-day-old pups revealed no homozygous mutant Mfn2 T105M mice and an abnormally low percentage of homozygous mutant Mfn2 R400Q mice, whereas mutant allele distribution of Mfn2 M376V mice followed Mendelian norms (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows genotype distribution data consistent with expected Mendelian ratios for M376V.

claim: No homozygous Mfn2 T105M mice were found as early as E12.5.
source: Analysis of embryos from timed crosses revealed no homozygous Mfn2 T105M mice as early as E12.5, recapitulating early embryonic lethality described in germline Mfn1 and Mfn2 knockout mice (Chen et al., 2003); heterozygous Mfn2 T105M mice had normal hearts and a neurological phenotype to be reported separately.
evidence: This is reported from timed breeding experiments and embryo genotyping.

claim: Homozygous Mfn2 T105M mice recapitulate early embryonic lethality described in germline Mfn1 and Mfn2 knockout mice.
source: Analysis of embryos from timed crosses revealed no homozygous Mfn2 T105M mice as early as E12.5, recapitulating early embryonic lethality described in germline Mfn1 and Mfn2 knockout mice (Chen et al., 2003); heterozygous Mfn2 T105M mice had normal hearts and a neurological phenotype to be reported separately.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2003 and the observed embryonic lethality.

claim: Heterozygous Mfn2 T105M mice had normal hearts.
source: Analysis of embryos from timed crosses revealed no homozygous Mfn2 T105M mice as early as E12.5, recapitulating early embryonic lethality described in germline Mfn1 and Mfn2 knockout mice (Chen et al., 2003); heterozygous Mfn2 T105M mice had normal hearts and a neurological phenotype to be reported separately.
evidence: This is reported from phenotypic analysis of heterozygous T105M mice.

claim: Heterozygous and homozygous Mfn2 M376V mice had normal hearts.
source: Heterozygous and homozygous Mfn2 M376V mice likewise had normal hearts.
evidence: This is reported from phenotypic analysis of M376V mice.

claim: Litter size from homozygous Mfn2 Q/Q400 crosses was normal at E18.5.
source: Litter size from homozygous crosses, reflecting survival of Q/Q400 mice, was normal at E18.5.
evidence: Figure 4C shows litter size data at E18.5.

claim: Approximately one-third of Q/Q400 fetuses died between E18.5 and birth (P0).
source: However, approximately one-third of Q/Q400 fetuses died between E18.5 and birth (P0), and another approximately one-third of Q/Q400 pups succumbed by P7, after which there was no further abnormal mortality (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows survival data demonstrating mortality between E18.5 and P0.

claim: Another approximately one-third of Q/Q400 pups succumbed by P7.
source: However, approximately one-third of Q/Q400 fetuses died between E18.5 and birth (P0), and another approximately one-third of Q/Q400 pups succumbed by P7, after which there was no further abnormal mortality (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows survival data demonstrating mortality between P0 and P7.

claim: After P7, there was no further abnormal mortality in Q/Q400 mice.
source: However, approximately one-third of Q/Q400 fetuses died between E18.5 and birth (P0), and another approximately one-third of Q/Q400 pups succumbed by P7, after which there was no further abnormal mortality (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows survival data with stable survival after P7.

claim: Over half of P0 Q/Q400 mouse hearts showed foci of cardiomyocyte vacuolation.
source: Histological examination of two litters of P0 Q/Q400 mice by a blinded Washington University veterinary pathologist revealed 'foci of cardiomyocyte vacuolation' in the myocardia of over half of the hearts (Figure 4D).
evidence: Figure 4D shows histological images and this is reported from pathological examination.

claim: No other organs besides the heart showed any histological or structural abnormalities in P0 Q/Q400 mice.
source: No other organs showed any histological or structural abnormalities.
evidence: This is reported from comprehensive histological examination of multiple organs.

claim: Ultrastructural examination of Q/Q400 hearts revealed loss of myofibrillar integrity with mitochondrial scarcity, disorganization, fragmentation, and degeneration.
source: Ultrastructural examination revealed loss of myofibrillar integrity with mitochondrial scarcity, disorganization, fragmentation, and degeneration (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Figure 4E shows transmission electron microscopy images demonstrating these ultrastructural abnormalities.

claim: Mfn2 Q/Q400 mice develop a highly specific, incompletely penetrant late fetal/early perinatal cardiomyopathy.
source: Thus, Mfn2 Q/Q400 mice develop a highly specific, incompletely penetrant late fetal/early perinatal cardiomyopathy.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data, histology, and electron microscopy showing cardiac-specific pathology with variable penetrance.

claim: Unsupervised clustering of dysregulated Q/Q400 cardiac mRNAs segregated hearts into those having near-normal mRNA levels (Q400n) and those manifesting an abnormal transcriptional profile (Q400a).
source: Unsupervised clustering of dysregulated Q/Q400 cardiac mRNAs (p-value<0.02, FDR < 0.05, fold change >2 vs. wild-type) segregated hearts into those having near-normal mRNA levels (designated nominal; Q400n) and those manifesting an abnormal transcriptional profile (designated anomalous; Q400a) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Figure 5A shows the heat map demonstrating this segregation pattern.

claim: mRNAs with lower expression in Q400a hearts were overwhelmingly categorized to metabolic and mitochondrial disease pathways.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of dysregulated Q400a transcripts categorized mRNAs with lower expression in Q400a hearts overwhelmingly to metabolic and mitochondrial disease pathways (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows pie charts of KEGG pathway analysis for downregulated genes.

claim: Genes with increased expression in Q400a hearts were linked to multiple injury responses.
source: By contrast, genes with increased expression in the same hearts were linked to multiple injury responses (Figure 5B), likely reflecting a compensatory reaction to myocardial degeneration.
evidence: Figure 5B shows pie charts of KEGG pathway analysis for upregulated genes.

claim: Metabolomics segregated MFN2 Q/Q400 mice into Q400a and Q400n groups.
source: The abnormal metabolic transcriptional signature of Q400a mouse hearts prompted metabolomics studies of individual newborn mouse hearts. As with gene expression, metabolomics segregated MFN2 Q/Q400 mice into Q400a and Q400n (Figure 5D).
evidence: Figure 5D shows the metabolomics heat map demonstrating this segregation pattern.

claim: Metabolic differentiation between Q400a and Q400n was largely driven by abnormally low levels of lactate in Q400a hearts.
source: Metabolic differentiation between Q400a and Q400n was largely driven by abnormally low levels of a preferred metabolic substrate for fetal myocardium, lactate (Lopaschuk et al., 1992; Piquereau and Ventura-Clapier, 2018) in Q400a hearts.
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 3 shows lactate levels and this is supported by citations to Lopaschuk et al., 1992 and Piquereau and Ventura-Clapier, 2018.

claim: Levels of C2 fatty acid acylcarnitines and several amino acids were diminished in Q400a hearts.
source: Levels of C2 fatty acid acylcarnitines and several amino acids were also diminished (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 3 shows metabolite level measurements.

claim: MFN2 Q400 fetal hearts showed broad downregulation of mRNAs encoding fatty acid entry, glycolysis, tricarboxylic cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation pathway proteins.
source: Specific interrogation of metabolic pathway gene expression in MFN2 Q400 fetal hears revealed broad downregulation of mRNAs encoding fatty acid entry, glycolysis, tricarboxylic cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation pathway proteins (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: Figure 5E-H shows gene expression data for these metabolic pathways.

claim: The development of cardiomyopathy in Mfn2 Q/Q400 fetuses and neonates corresponds with signature abnormalities of myocardial metabolism.
source: Thus, the development of cardiomyopathy in Mfn2 Q/Q400 fetuses and neonates corresponds with signature abnormalities of myocardial metabolism.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective RNA-seq and metabolomics data presented in Figure 5.

claim: The MFN2 Q400 fetal heart profile of abnormal metabolic gene expression recapitulates transcriptional changes evoked by experimentally interrupting MFN2-Parkin-mediated mitophagy in perinatal hearts.
source: This notion gained support from our observation that the MFN2 Q400 fetal heart profile of abnormal fatty acid entry, glycolysis, tricarboxylic cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation pathway gene expression (see Figure 5) recapitulates transcriptional changes evoked by experimentally interrupting MFN2-Parkin-mediated mitophagy in perinatal hearts (Gong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the current data with published data from Gong et al., 2015.

claim: The MFN2 Q400 mRNA profile has little similarity to the transcriptional signature provoked by suppressing mitochondrial fusion in embryonic myocardium.
source: Importantly, this mRNA profile has little similarity to the transcriptional signature provoked by suppressing mitochondrial fusion in embryonic myocardium (Kasahara et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the current data with published data from Kasahara et al., 2013.

claim: Each stage of mitophagy (Parkin recruitment, autophagosome engulfment, lysosomal delivery) was markedly delayed in H9C2 cells expressing MFN2 Q400.
source: Remarkably, each of the stages of mitophagy was markedly delayed in H9C2 cells expressing MFN2 Q400 at an equivalent level (Figure 6C).
evidence: Figure 6C shows time-course data for all three stages of mitophagy demonstrating delays in Q400-expressing cells.

claim: Mitophagy slowly increased over longer time periods in MFN2 Q400 cells, likely reflecting MFN2-independent mitochondrial Parkin recruitment.
source: Mitophagy slowly increased over longer time periods in MFN2 Q400 cells, likely reflecting MFN2-independent mitochondrial Parkin recruitment (Ordureau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the time-course data and supported by citation to Ordureau et al., 2014.

claim: CMT2A-associated MFN2 T105M and M376A expressed in H9c2 cells promoted normal FCCP-stimulated Parkin recruitment to mitochondria.
source: As in Mfn2 DKO cells (see Figure 3C), CMT2A-associated MFN2 T105M and M376A expressed in H9c2 cells promoted normal FCCP-stimulated Parkin recruitment to mitochondria, whereas Parkin aggregation was impaired in cardiomyoblasts expressing MFN2 R400Q (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A); mitophagy measured as mitolysosome formation followed the same pattern (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 6D shows Parkin aggregation data in H9c2 cells for these mutants.

claim: Parkin aggregation was impaired in H9c2 cardiomyoblasts expressing MFN2 R400Q.
source: As in Mfn2 DKO cells (see Figure 3C), CMT2A-associated MFN2 T105M and M376A expressed in H9c2 cells promoted normal FCCP-stimulated Parkin recruitment to mitochondria, whereas Parkin aggregation was impaired in cardiomyoblasts expressing MFN2 R400Q (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A); mitophagy measured as mitolysosome formation followed the same pattern (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 6D shows reduced Parkin aggregation data in H9c2 cells expressing R400Q.

claim: Mitophagy-defective MFN2 Q400 was less effective than WT MFN2 R400 in promoting H9c2 cardiomyoblast mitochondrial respiration.
source: Mitophagy-defective MFN2 Q400 was less effective than WT MFN2 R400 in promoting H9c2 cardiomyoblast mitochondrial respiration (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), recapitulating its effects in MEFs (see Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 2 shows Seahorse respiration data in H9c2 cells.

claim: Developmentally regulated Mfn2-Parkin-mediated mitophagy is essential for myocardial metabolic maturation in the perinatal period.
source: Based on prior reports (Gong et al., 2015), developmentally regulated Mfn2-Parkin-mediated mitophagy is essential for myocardial metabolic maturation in the perinatal period, whereas in adult hearts the same mitophagy mechanism mediates mitochondrial quality control (Song et al., 2015; Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gong et al., 2015; Song et al., 2015; and Song et al., 2017.

claim: In adult hearts, Mfn2-Parkin-mediated mitophagy mediates mitochondrial quality control.
source: Based on prior reports (Gong et al., 2015), developmentally regulated Mfn2-Parkin-mediated mitophagy is essential for myocardial metabolic maturation in the perinatal period, whereas in adult hearts the same mitophagy mechanism mediates mitochondrial quality control (Song et al., 2015; Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Song et al., 2015 and Song et al., 2017.

claim: Doxorubicin is an anti-cancer chemotherapeutic with well-characterized dose-dependent cardiotoxic effects mediated in large part by mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Doxorubicin, an anti-cancer chemotherapeutic with well-characterized dose-dependent cardiotoxic effects mediated in large part by mitochondrial dysfunction (Wallace et al., 2020; Schirone et al., 2022), is such an insult.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wallace et al., 2020 and Schirone et al., 2022.

claim: Expression of MFN2 Q400 increased overall doxorubicin-stimulated H9c2 cell death.
source: Expression of MFN2 Q400 increased overall doxorubicin-stimulated H9c2 cell death and TUNEL apoptosis marker labeling (Figure 7A and B), while suppressing mitochondrial Parkin recruitment and mitolysosome formation (Figure 7C).
evidence: Figure 7A shows dose-response curves demonstrating increased cell death with Q400.

claim: Expression of MFN2 Q400 increased TUNEL apoptosis marker labeling in doxorubicin-treated H9c2 cells.
source: Expression of MFN2 Q400 increased overall doxorubicin-stimulated H9c2 cell death and TUNEL apoptosis marker labeling (Figure 7A and B), while suppressing mitochondrial Parkin recruitment and mitolysosome formation (Figure 7C).
evidence: Figure 7B shows TUNEL labeling data demonstrating increased apoptosis with Q400.

claim: Expression of MFN2 Q400 suppressed mitochondrial Parkin recruitment and mitolysosome formation in doxorubicin-treated H9c2 cells.
source: Expression of MFN2 Q400 increased overall doxorubicin-stimulated H9c2 cell death and TUNEL apoptosis marker labeling (Figure 7A and B), while suppressing mitochondrial Parkin recruitment and mitolysosome formation (Figure 7C).
evidence: Figure 7C shows Parkin aggregation and mitolysosome formation data in doxorubicin-treated cells.

claim: Expression of MFN2 Q400 increased baseline mitochondrial ROS to levels comparable to those provoked by doxorubicin in normal cells.
source: Compared to WT MFN2 R400, expression of MFN2 Q400 increased baseline mitochondrial ROS to levels comparable to those provoked by doxorubicin in normal cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: Figure 7D shows flow cytometry data of MitoSOX fluorescence demonstrating elevated baseline ROS with Q400.

claim: Homozygous Mfn2 Q/Q400 knock-in mice had greater increases in left ventricular chamber dimension and calculated LV mass after doxorubicin than WT or heterozygous mice.
source: Left ventricular (LV) chamber dimension at end-diastole (LVEDD) and calculated LV mass increased, and LV ejection performance (fractional shortening; FS) decreased to a greater extent in homozygous Mfn2 Q/Q 400 knock-in mice than WT or heterozygous mice (Figure 7E).
evidence: Figure 7E shows echocardiography data demonstrating greater cardiac dysfunction in Q/Q400 mice after doxorubicin.

claim: LV ejection performance (fractional shortening) decreased to a greater extent in homozygous Mfn2 Q/Q400 knock-in mice than WT or heterozygous mice after doxorubicin.
source: Left ventricular (LV) chamber dimension at end-diastole (LVEDD) and calculated LV mass increased, and LV ejection performance (fractional shortening; FS) decreased to a greater extent in homozygous Mfn2 Q/Q 400 knock-in mice than WT or heterozygous mice (Figure 7E).
evidence: Figure 7E shows echocardiography data demonstrating greater reduction in fractional shortening in Q/Q400 mice after doxorubicin.

claim: Gravimetric heart weights were greater in doxorubicin-treated Mfn2 Q/Q400 mice than the other groups.
source: Likewise, gravimetric heart weights were greater in doxorubicin-treated Mfn2 Q/Q400 mice than the other groups (Figure 7F).
evidence: Figure 7F shows heart weight data indexed to tibial length.

claim: The exaggerated Mfn2 Q/Q400 mouse cardiotoxic response to doxorubicin was associated with diminished reactive mitophagy.
source: As in cultured H9c2 cardiomyoblasts, the exaggerated Mfn2 Q/Q400 mouse cardiotoxic response to doxorubicin was associated with diminished reactive mitophagy (Figure 7G).
evidence: Figure 7G shows MitoQC visualization data demonstrating reduced mitolysosome formation in Q/Q400 hearts after doxorubicin.

claim: Conventional hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies are caused by mutations of sarcomeric proteins.
source: Conventional hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies are caused by mutations of sarcomeric proteins (Mazzarotto et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mazzarotto et al., 2020.

claim: Myocardial-specific clinical disease can be induced by mutational disruption of mitophagy.
source: The current data suggest that myocardial-specific clinical disease can also be induced by mutational disruption of mitophagy.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective data presented in the manuscript showing cardiac-specific pathology associated with mitophagy defects.

claim: Non-phosphorylated WT MFN2 promotes MFN-MFN-mediated fusion, but cannot bind Parkin, while MFN2 phosphorylation on S378 extinguishes fusion and on T111 and S442 enables Parkin binding to initiate mitophagy.
source: Under normal circumstances, mitofusin–mitofusin binding mediates mitochondrial fusion, and mitofusin–Parkin binding promotes mitophagy; these are mutually exclusive functions regulated by PINK1 kinase (Li et al., 2022). Thus, non-phosphorylated WT MFN2 promotes MFN-MFN-mediated fusion, but cannot bind Parkin. MFN2 phosphorylation on S378 extinguishes fusion (Rocha et al., 2018) and on T111 and S442 enables Parkin binding to initiate mitophagy (Chen and Dorn, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2022; Rocha et al., 2018; and Chen and Dorn, 2013.

claim: MFN2 phosphorylation and its control of mitochondrial fate are mechanistically linked by altered MFN2 protein partnering as a consequence of phosphorylation-induced changes in MFN2 conformation.
source: MFN2 phosphorylation on these residues and its control of mitochondrial fate are mechanistically linked by altered MFN2 protein partnering as a consequence of phosphorylation-induced changes in MFN2 conformation (Dorn, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dorn, 2020.

claim: Lack of conformational malleability did not distinguish between the cardiomyopathy- vs. the neuropathy-associated MFN2 mutants.
source: Lack of conformational malleability did not distinguish between the cardiomyopathy- vs. the neuropathy-associated MFN2 mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data showing both R400Q and M376A have impaired conformational switching, yet only R400Q is associated with cardiomyopathy.

claim: Mitochondrial depolarization (rather than just fragmentation) may play an important pathological role in CMT2A, but not cardiomyopathy.
source: These findings suggest that mitochondrial depolarization (rather than just fragmentation) may play an important pathological role in CMT2A, but not cardiomyopathy.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the depolarization patterns (Figure 2B) with the disease phenotypes observed in the knock-in mice.

claim: The low prevalence of MFN2 R400Q compared to non-synonymous MFN2 mutations in the same HR1 domain could reflect negative selection throughout modern human evolution of an ancient and harmful gene variant.
source: It is worth considering that the low prevalence of this mutation compared to non-synonymous MFN2 mutations in the same HR1 domain, and its over-representation in individuals of African descent, could also reflect negative selection throughout modern human evolution of an ancient and harmful gene variant.
evidence: This is presented as speculation based on the population genetics data.

claim: Different patterns of mitofusin dysfunction underlie organ-specific manifestations of clinical diseases caused by MFN2 mutations.
source: Finally, our data support the concept that different patterns of mitofusin dysfunction underlie organ-specific manifestations of clinical diseases caused by MFN2 mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective data showing different functional defects (motility vs. mitophagy) correlating with different organ involvement (nerve vs. heart).
